questions.question: Consider the matrix \[\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 & 4 \\ -1 & -1 & -2 \end{pmatrix}\] whose eigenvalues are \(1, -1\) and \(3\). Then Trace of \((\mathbf{A}^3 - 3\mathbf{A}^2)\) is .
questions.explanation:
If \(\lambda\) is an eigenvalue of a matrix \(A\), then by polynomial matrix properties, \(\lambda^3 - 3\lambda^2\) is an eigenvalue of the matrix \(A^3 - 3A^2\). Given that \(\lambda = 1, -1,\) and \(3\) are the particular eigenvalues of a matrix \(A_{3 \times 3}\), we compute the corresponding eigenvalues for the matrix \(A^3 - 3A^2\):
  • For \(\lambda = 1\): \[\lambda^3 - 3\lambda^2 = (1)^3 - 3(1)^2 = 1 - 3 = -2\]
  • For \(\lambda = -1\): \[\lambda^3 - 3\lambda^2 = (-1)^3 - 3(-1)^2 = -1 - 3 = -4\]
  • For \(\lambda = 3\): \[\lambda^3 - 3\lambda^2 = (3)^3 - 3(3)^2 = 27 - 27 = 0\]
The particular eigenvalues of the matrix \(A^3 - 3A^2\) are \(-2, -4,\) and \(0\). We know that the trace of a matrix is equal to the sum of its eigenvalues: \[\text{Trace}(A^3 - 3A^2) = (-2) + (-4) + 0 = \boxed{-6}\]
Key points
  • Eigenvalue Polynomial Property: If a square matrix \(A\) has eigenvalues \(\lambda_i\), then any matrix polynomial \(f(A)\) has corresponding eigenvalues \(f(\lambda_i)\).
  • Trace Property: The trace of any square matrix (\(\text{Tr}(M)\)) is identically equal to the sum of all its eigenvalues.

questions.explanation: Given the equation of the straight line is: \[y = mx + c\] Since the line passes through the origin \((0, 0)\), we can substitute \(x = 0\) and \(y = 0\) into the equation: \[0 = m(0) + c \implies c = 0\] Thus, the equation of the line simplifies to: \[y = mx\] The line also passes through the point \((x, y) = (2, 6)\). Substituting these values into the simplified equation gives: \[6 = m(2)\] \[m = \frac{6}{2} = 3\] \[\boxed{3}\]

questions.question: \(\lim_{n \to \infty} \left( \sqrt{n^2 + n} - \sqrt{n^2 + 1} \right)\) is .
questions.explanation: We need to evaluate the limit: \[L = \lim_{n \to \infty} \left( \sqrt{n^2 + n} - \sqrt{n^2 + 1} \right)\] To resolve the \(\infty - \infty\) form, we rationalize the expression by multiplying and dividing by its conjugate: \[L = \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{\left(\sqrt{n^2 + n} - \sqrt{n^2 + 1}\right)\left(\sqrt{n^2 + n} + \sqrt{n^2 + 1}\right)}{\sqrt{n^2 + n} + \sqrt{n^2 + 1}}\] \[L = \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{(n^2 + n) - (n^2 + 1)}{\sqrt{n^2 + n} + \sqrt{n^2 + 1}}\] \[L = \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{n - 1}{\sqrt{n^2 + n} + \sqrt{n^2 + 1}}\] Factoring out \(n\) from both the numerator and the denominator: \[L = \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{n\left(1 - \frac{1}{n}\right)}{n\left(\sqrt{1 + \frac{1}{n}} + \sqrt{1 + \frac{1}{n^2}}\right)}\] \[L = \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{1 - \frac{1}{n}}{\sqrt{1 + \frac{1}{n}} + \sqrt{1 + \frac{1}{n^2}}}\] Evaluating the limit as \(n \to \infty\): \[L = \frac{1 - 0}{\sqrt{1 + 0} + \sqrt{1 + 0}} = \frac{1}{1 + 1} = \frac{1}{2} = 0.5\] \[\boxed{0.5}\]

questions.question: Let \(f \colon [-1, 1] \to \mathbb{R}\), where \(f(x) = 2x^3 - x^4 - 10\). The minimum value of \(f(x)\) is .
questions.explanation:
The given function is: \[f(x) = 2x^3 - x^4 - 10 \quad \text{for } x \in [-1, 1]\] To find the minimum value of \(f(x)\) on a closed interval, we must evaluate the function at its critical points within the interval and at the boundaries of the interval. First, let's find the first derivative of \(f(x)\) with respect to \(x\): \[f'(x) = 6x^2 - 4x^3\] Set \(f'(x) = 0\) to find the stationary points: \[2x^2(3 - 2x) = 0\] \[x = 0 \quad \text{or} \quad x = \frac{3}{2} = 1.5\] Since the given domain is \([-1, 1]\), the stationary point \(x = 1.5\) lies outside the interval and will not be considered. The only valid stationary point inside the domain is \(x = 0\). Now, evaluate \(f(x)\) at the critical point \(x = 0\) and at the boundary points \(x = -1\) and \(x = 1\): \[\begin{aligned} f(-1) &= 2(-1)^3 - (-1)^4 - 10 = -2 - 1 - 10 = -13 \\ f(1) &= 2(1)^3 - (1)^4 - 10 = 2 - 1 - 10 = -9 \\ f(0) &= 2(0)^3 - (0)^4 - 10 = -10 \end{aligned}\] Comparing these values, the minimum value of \(f(x)\) in the interval \([-1, 1]\) is: \[\min\{f(-1), f(1), f(0)\} = \min\{-13, -9, -10\} = -13\] \[\boxed{-13}\]
Mistakes to avoid
Always remember to check the boundaries of the closed interval \([-1, 1]\). Relying solely on local extrema conditions at stationary points (like \(x=0\)) can lead to missing the global minimum which happens to occur at the boundary \(x = -1\).

questions.question: The value of the integral \(\dfrac{1}{2\pi j} \oint_{C} \dfrac{z^2+1}{z^2-1} \, dz\) where \(z\) is a complex number and \(C\) is a unit circle with center at \(1+0j\) in the complex plane is .
questions.explanation:
To evaluate the following, \[I = \frac{1}{2\pi j} \oint_{C} \frac{z^2 + 1}{z^2 - 1} \, dz\] To find the poles, \[z^2 - 1 = (z - 1)(z + 1)\] The simple poles are at \(z = 1\) and \(z = -1\). The contour \(C\) is a unit circle centered at \(1 + 0j = 1\). Its equation is: \[|z - 1| = 1\]
  • For \(z = 1\): \(|1 - 1| = 0 < 1\) \(\implies z = 1\) lies inside the contour \(C\).
  • For \(z = -1\): \(|-1 - 1| = |-2| = 2 > 1\) \(\implies z = -1\) lies outside the contour \(C\).
Apply Cauchy's Integral Formula to \(z = 1\) : \[\oint_{C} \frac{\frac{z^2 + 1}{z + 1}}{z - 1} \, dz\] Let \(f(z) = \frac{z^2 + 1}{z + 1}\), which is analytic within and on the contour \(C\). By Cauchy's Integral Formula: \[\oint_{C} \frac{f(z)}{z - 1} \, dz = 2\pi j \cdot f(1)\] Finding \(f(1)\): \[f(1) = \frac{1^2 + 1}{1 + 1} = \frac{2}{2} = 1\] Substituting this back into our calculation: \[\oint_{C} \frac{z^2 + 1}{z^2 - 1} \, dz = 2\pi j \cdot (1) = 2\pi j\] Substitute the contour integral value back into the original expression: \[I = \frac{1}{2\pi j} \cdot (2\pi j) = 1\] \[\boxed{1}\]

P(R_2|R_1)P(R_1)
+
P(R_2|G_1)P(G_1)\] \[=
\frac{6}{13}\cdot\frac{5}{12}
+
\frac{5}{13}\cdot\frac{7}{12}\] \[=
\frac{30+35}{156}
=
\frac{65}{156}.\] \[\boxed{\text{(a) }\frac{65}{156}}\]

questions.question: For the periodic signal \(x(t)\) shown below with period \(T=8~\text{s}\), the power in the \(10^{\text{th}}\) harmonic is
questions.explanation:
Theory: A periodic signal with half-wave symmetry contains only odd harmonics; all even harmonics are absent. From the waveform,\[x\!\left(t+\frac{T}{2}\right)=-x(t),\]which indicates half-wave symmetry. Hence, \[\text{All even harmonic Fourier coefficients are zero.}\]Since the \(10^{\text{th}}\) harmonic is an even harmonic,\[C_{10}=0.\]Therefore, the power in the \(10^{\text{th}}\) harmonic is \[P_{10}=|C_{10}|^2=0.\] \[\boxed{\text{(A) }0}\]
Key points
  • Half-wave symmetry eliminates all even harmonics.
  • Harmonic power is zero whenever the corresponding Fourier coefficient is zero.
  • Only odd harmonics contribute to the Fourier series of this waveform.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not compute Fourier coefficients unnecessarily after identifying half-wave symmetry.
  • Do not confuse odd symmetry with half-wave symmetry.
  • Remember that the \(10^{\text{th}}\) harmonic is an even harmonic.

questions.explanation:
Theory: The final value theorem gives the steady-state value of a signal provided all poles of \(sX(s)\) lie in the left half-plane. Using the final value theorem,\[\lim_{t\to\infty}x(t) = \lim_{s\to0}sX(s).\]Substituting the given transform,\[\lim_{t\to\infty}x(t) = \lim_{s\to0} \frac{s(s+2)}{(s+1)(s+3)^2}.\]Evaluating at \(s=0\),\[\lim_{t\to\infty}x(t) = \frac{0\cdot2}{1\cdot9} = 0.\]Hence,\[\boxed{\text{}0}\]
Key points
  • Use the final value theorem only after verifying its applicability.
  • Compute \(\displaystyle \lim_{s\to0}sX(s)\).
  • All poles of \(sX(s)\) must lie in the left half-plane.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not apply the theorem if right-half-plane or imaginary-axis poles are present.
  • Multiply by \(s\) before taking the limit.
  • Substitute \(s=0\) only after forming \(sX(s)\).

questions.question: An ideal opamp is used to realize a difference amplifier circuit given below having a gain of \(10\). If \(x = 0.025\), the CMRR of the circuit in dB is .
questions.explanation: Let \[R_{1}=10(1-x)\,\text{k}\Omega,\quad R_{2}=10(1+x)\,\text{k}\Omega,\] \[R_{3}=100(1-x)\,\text{k}\Omega,\quad R_{F}=100(1+x)\,\text{k}\Omega.\] Here, \[R_{F}=10R_{2}, \qquad R_{3}=10R_{1}.\] For a practical difference amplifier with resistor mismatch, \[\mathrm{CMRR} = -\frac{1}{2} \left[ \frac{(R_{1}+R_{F})R_{3}+R_{F}(R_{2}+R_{3})} {(R_{1}+R_{F})R_{3}-R_{F}(R_{2}+R_{3})} \right].\] Substituting \(R_{F}=10R_{2}\) and \(R_{3}=10R_{1}\), \[\mathrm{CMRR} = -\frac{1}{2} \left[ \frac{R_{1}^{2}+R_{2}^{2}+20R_{1}R_{2}} {R_{1}^{2}-R_{2}^{2}} \right].\] Since \[R_{1}=10(1-x),\qquad R_{2}=10(1+x),\] \[\mathrm{CMRR} = -\frac{1}{2} \left[ \frac{(1+x)^2+(1-x)^2+20(1-x^2)} {(1-x)^2-(1+x)^2} \right].\] For \(x=0.025\), \[\mathrm{CMRR}=110.\] Hence, \[\mathrm{CMRR}_{\mathrm{dB}} = 20\log_{10}(110) = 40.83\,\text{dB}.\] \[\boxed{40.83}\]

questions.question: A 1 Kbyte memory module has to be interfaced with an 8-bit microprocessor that has 16 address lines. The address lines \(A_0\) to \(A_9\) of the processor are connected to the corresponding address lines of the memory. The active low chip select \(\overline{\text{CS}}\) of the memory module is connected to the \(y_5\) output of a 3-to-8 decoder with active low outputs. \(S_0\) , \(S_1\) and \(S_2\) are the input lines to the decoder, with \(S_2\) as the MSB. The decoder has one active low \(\overline{\text{EN}_1}\) and one active high \(\text{EN}_2\) enable lines as shown below. The address range(s) that gets mapped onto this memory module is/are
questions.explanation:
The given interfacing circuit uses a decoder with select lines \(S_0, S_1, S_2\) connected to address lines \(A_{12}, A_{13}, A_{14}\), and outputs \(y_0\) through \(y_7\), with \(\overline{CS}\) activated via output \(y_5\). The chip should be selected when \(y_5\) is active, which requires: \[A_{14}A_{13}A_{12} = 101\] For the decoder's enable inputs: \(EN_2\) to be active requires \(A_{11} = 1\), and \(\overline{EN_1}\) to be active requires \(A_{10} = 0\). Combining these conditions: \[\begin{array}{ccccc} A_{14} & A_{13} & A_{12} & A_{11} & A_{10} \\ \hline 1 & 0 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ \end{array}\] With \(A_{15} = 0\) or \(A_{15} = 1\) as the remaining free bit, and all unspecified lower-order address bits (\(A_9\) through \(A_0\)) ranging from all 0s to all 1s, the two possible address ranges are: For \(A_{15} = 0\): \[0\;1\;0\;1\;1\;0\;0\;0\;\cdots 0 = 5800\text{H} \quad \text{to} \quad 0\;1\;0\;1\;1\;0\;1\;1\;\cdots 1 = 5BFF\text{H}\] For \(A_{15} = 1\): \[1\;1\;0\;1\;1\;0\;0\;0\;\cdots 0 = D800\text{H} \quad \text{to} \quad 1\;1\;0\;1\;1\;0\;1\;1\;\cdots 1 = DBFF\text{H}\] \[\boxed{(D) \text{ 5800H to 5BFFH and D800H to DBFFH}}\]
Key points
  • The chip-select address decoding logic fixes certain address bits (those connected to decoder select lines and enable inputs) while leaving the remaining bits free; the free bits define the size and range of the addressable memory block.
  • Any address bit not connected to the decoder (here \(A_{15}\) and \(A_9\) through \(A_0\)) can take any value, producing multiple valid address ranges (aliasing) for the same physical memory chip.
  • The size of the address range is determined by the number of free (unconnected) lower-order bits: here \(10\) free bits (\(A_9\)--\(A_0\)) give a block size of \(2^{10} = 1024\) bytes (\(400\text{H}\)), matching the range \(5800\text{H}\) to \(5BFF\text{H}\).
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not assume a single unique address range; unconnected high-order bits (like \(A_{15}\) here) create multiple aliased address ranges for the same chip, all of which are valid answers.
  • Carefully distinguish between address bits used for decoding (fixed values determined by the circuit) and bits left floating/unused (free to vary, creating the address range span).
  • Double-check the decoder's enable polarity (\(EN_2\) active-high requires \(A_{11}=1\); \(\overline{EN_1}\) active-low requires \(A_{10}=0\)) --- reversing these conditions would shift the address range entirely.

questions.question: The relationship between the force \(f(t)\) and the displacement \(x(t)\) of a spring-mass system (with a mass \(M\), viscous damping \(D\) and spring constant \(K\)) is \[M\frac{d^2x(t)}{dt^2} + D\frac{dx(t)}{dt} + Kx(t) = f(t) .\] \(X(s)\) and \(F(s)\) are the Laplace transforms of \(x(t)\) and \(f(t)\) respectively. With \(M = 0.1\), \(D = 2\), \(K = 10\) in appropriate units, the transfer function \(G(s) = \dfrac{X(s)}{F(s)}\) is
questions.explanation:
The given differential equation : \[M\dfrac{d^2x(t)}{dt^2} + D\dfrac{dx(t)}{dt} + Kx(t) = f(t)\] Taking the Laplace transform on both sides under zero initial conditions: \[M s^2 X(s) + D s X(s) + K X(s) = F(s)\] \[\left(M s^2 + D s + K\right) X(s) = F(s)\] Thus, the transfer function \(G(s)\) is: \[G(s) = \dfrac{X(s)}{F(s)} = \dfrac{1}{M s^2 + D s + K}\] Substituting the given parameters \(M = 0.1\), \(D = 2\), and \(K = 10\): \[G(s) = \frac{1}{0.1s^2 + 2s + 10} = \frac{10}{s^2 + 20s + 100}\] \[\boxed{(A) \ \ \dfrac{10}{s^2 + 20s + 100}}\]
Key points
The transfer function is always defined assuming all initial conditions are zero.

questions.subject: control-systems
questions.question: Match the unit-step responses (1), (2) and (3) with the transfer functions \(P(s)\), \(Q(s)\) and \(R(s)\), given below. \[P(s) = \frac{-1}{(s + 1)}; \ Q(s) = \frac{2(s - 1)}{(s + 10)(s + 2)}; \ R(s) = \frac{1}{(s + 1)^2}\]
questions.note: Marks awarded to all (official key: MTA)
questions.explanation:
The input is a unit-step signal, so \(U(s) = \dfrac{1}{s}\). The steady-state value \(c(\infty)\) is given by: \[c(\infty) = \lim_{s \to 0} s \cdot C(s) = \lim_{s \to 0} s \cdot H(s) \cdot U(s) = \lim_{s \to 0} H(s)\] For \(P(s)\):
\[P(s) = \frac{-1}{s + 1}\] \[c(\infty) = \lim_{s \to 0} \frac{-1}{s + 1} = -1\] This matches curve (1). For \(Q(s)\):
\[Q(s) = \frac{2(s - 1)}{(s + 10)(s + 2)}\] \[c(\infty) = \lim_{s \to 0} \frac{2(s - 1)}{(s + 10)(s + 2)}= -0.5\] Doesn't match any option For \(R(s)\):
\[R(s) = \frac{1}{(s + 1)^2}\] \[c(\infty) = \lim_{s \to 0} \frac{1}{(s + 1)^2} = 1\] This matches curve (3).
Key points
For a unit-step input \(U(s) = \dfrac{1}{s}\), the steady-state output value equals the DC gain of the system, i.e., \(c(\infty) = H(0)\).

questions.subject: control-systems
questions.question: The value of \(a_0\) which will ensure that the polynomial \(s^3 + 3s^2 + 2s + a_0\) has roots on the left half of the \(s\)-plane is
questions.explanation:
For roots to lie strictly in the left half of the \(s\)-plane, all coefficients must be positive, meaning \(a_0 > 0\).
Method 1
Using the Routh-Hurwitz criterion:
\(s^3\)\(1\)\(2\)
\(s^2\)\(3\)\(a_0\)
\(s^1\)\(\dfrac{6 - a_0}{3}\)\(0\)
\(s^0\)\(a_0\)
For stability, the \(s^1\) row element must be positive: \[\frac{6 - a_0}{3} > 0 \implies a_0 < 6\] Combining conditions: \(0 < a_0 < 6\).
Method 2
For a stable third-order polynomial \(s^3 + a_2 s^2 + a_1 s + a_0 = 0\), the necessary and sufficient condition is: \[\text{Inner Product} > \text{Outer Product}\] \[a_2 a_1 > a_3 a_0\] Substituting the given parameters: \[3 \times 2 > 1 \times a_0 \implies 6 > a_0\] Thus, for stability, we must have \(a_0 < 6\).
\[\boxed{(D) \ \ 5}\]

questions.subject: control-systems
questions.question: For the feedback system given below, the transfer func- tion \(G(s) = \dfrac{1}{(s+1)^2}\). The system CANNOT be stabilized with
questions.explanation: The closed-loop characteristic equation is given by \(1 + C(s)G(s) = 0\), \[where, \ \ G(s) = \dfrac{1}{(s+1)^2} = \dfrac{1}{s^2 + 2s + 1}\] For a standard third-order characteristic equation \(s^3 + a_2 s^2 + a_1 s + a_0 = 0\), the system is stable if all coefficients are positive and satisfies the following stability condition: \[\text{Inner Product} > \text{Outer Product} \implies a_2 a_1 > a_0\] Option (A): For \(C(s) = \dfrac{s+3}{s}\): \[1+\dfrac{s+3}{s(s^2 + 2s + 1)}=0\] \[s^3 + 2s^2 + 2s + 3 = 0\] Checking stability: \[a_2 a_1 = 2 \times 2 = 4\] \[a_0 = 3\] Since \(4 > 3\), stable. Option (B): For \(C(s) = \dfrac{3s+7}{s}\): \[1+\dfrac{3s+7}{s(s^2 + 2s + 1)}=0\] \[s^3 + 2s^2 + 4s + 7 = 0\] Checking stability: \[a_2 a_1 = 2 \times 4 = 8\] \[a_0 = 7\] Since \(8 > 7\),stable. Option (C): For \(C(s) = \dfrac{3s+9}{s}\): \[1+\dfrac{3s+9}{s(s^2 + 2s + 1)}=0\] \[s^3 + 2s^2 + 4s + 9 = 0\] Checking stability: \[a_2 a_1 = 2 \times 4 = 8\] \[a_0 = 9\] Since \(8 \ngtr 9\), unstable. Option (D): For \(C(s) = \dfrac{1}{s}\): \[1+\dfrac{1}{s(s^2 + 2s + 1)}=0\] \[s^3 + 2s^2 + s + 1 = 0\] Checking stability: \[a_2 a_1 = 2 \times 1 = 2\] \[a_0 = 1\] Since \(2 > 1\), stable. \[\boxed{(C) \ \ C(s) = 3 + \dfrac{9}{s}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Which of the following is CORRECT with respect to grammar and usage? Mount Everest is _______.
options: the highest peak in the world
one of highest peak in the world
one of the highest peak in the world
questions.explanation:
``Mount Everest is ________'' requires the correct use of the superlative with the definite article.
  • A. the highest peak in the world — correct use of superlative with definite article the. \(\checkmark\)
  • B. highest peak in the world — missing definite article the before superlative.
  • C. one of highest peak in the world — missing article before highest and peak should be plural (peaks).
  • D. one of the highest peak in the world — peak must be plural: ``one of the highest peaks''.
\[\boxed{\text{A) the highest peak in the world}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: The policeman asked the victim of a theft, ``What did you _____?''
questions.explanation:
The policeman asked what the victim did — the blank must be a past-tense verb meaning ``to misplace or be deprived of something''.
  • A. loose — adjective meaning not tight; wrong part of speech.
  • B. lose — verb meaning to be deprived of something; correct in context. \(\checkmark\)
  • C. loss — noun; cannot fill a verb slot.
  • D. louse — an insect; completely unrelated.
\[\boxed{\text{B) lose}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Despite the new medicine's ______ in treating diabetes, it is not ______ widely.
questions.explanation:
The sentence provided is: "Despite the new medicine's ___________ in treating diabetes, it is not ___________ widely." Let us evaluate the options:
  • Option A (effectiveness --- prescribed): This forms a cohesive and logical contrast. "Despite the new medicine's effectiveness in treating diabetes, it is not prescribed widely." This accurately reflects standard medical phrasing where an effective drug faces prescription barriers.
  • Option B (availability --- used): If a medicine is widely available, there is no inherent logical paradox or strong conversational contrast to state that it is not used widely.
  • Option C (prescription --- available): "Prescription" does not syntactically fit as a characteristic quality belonging to the medicine in the first blank segment.
  • Option D (acceptance --- proscribed): "Proscribed" means officially forbidden or banned. Saying a medicine is not banned widely creates a double negative that violates the intuitive intent of the sentence.
\[\boxed{\text{A) effectiveness --- prescribed}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question:
In a world filled with uncertainty, he was glad to have many good friends. He had always assisted them in times of need and was confident that they would reciprocate. However, the events of the last week proved him wrong. Which of the following inference(s) is/are logically valid and can be inferred from the above passage?
  1. His friends were always asking him to help them.
  2. He felt that when in need of help, his friends would let him down.
  3. He was sure that his friends would help him when in need.
  4. His friends did not help him last week.
questions.explanation:
The passage states the person was ``glad to have many good friends'', had always assisted them, was confident they would reciprocate, but ``the events of the last week proved him wrong''. Evaluating each inference:
  1. His friends were always asking him to help them — not stated; we only know he always helped them.
  2. He felt that when in need of help, his friends would let him down — contradicts the passage (he was confident they would reciprocate).
  3. He was sure that his friends would help him when in need — directly supported by ``confident that they would reciprocate''. \(\checkmark\)
  4. His friends did not help him last week — directly supported by ``events of the last week proved him wrong''. \(\checkmark\)
\[\boxed{\text{B) (iii) and (iv)}}\]
Key points
  • An inference is valid only if it is directly supported by the passage without contradiction.
  • ``Proved him wrong'' \(\Rightarrow\) the reciprocation he expected did not happen.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Leela is older than her cousin Pavithra. Pavithra's brother Shiva is older than Leela. When Pavithra and Shiva are visiting Leela, all three like to play chess. Pavithra wins more often than Leela does. Which one of the following statements must be TRUE based on the above?
options: When Shiva plays chess with Leela and Pavithra, he often loses.
Leela is the oldest of the three.
Shiva is a better chess player than Pavithra.
Pavithra is the youngest of the three.
questions.explanation:
Establish the age ordering from the given facts:
  • Leela is older than Pavithra \(\Rightarrow\) Leela \(>\) Pavithra.
  • Pavithra's brother Shiva is older than Leela \(\Rightarrow\) Shiva \(>\) Leela \(>\) Pavithra.
Combined order: \[\text{Shiva} > \text{Leela} > \text{Pavithra}\] Pavithra wins chess more often than Leela — chess skill is independent of age order. Evaluating each option:
  • A. Shiva often loses when playing with Leela and Pavithra — not inferable from age or chess data.
  • B. Leela is the oldest — contradicted by Shiva \(>\) Leela.
  • C. Shiva is a better chess player than Pavithra — chess skill not related to age; not inferable.
  • D. Pavithra is the youngest of the three — directly follows from Shiva \(>\) Leela \(>\) Pavithra. \(\checkmark\)
\[\boxed{\text{D) Pavithra is the youngest of the three}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: The unruly crowd demanded that the accused be _____ without trial.
questions.explanation:
The crowd demanded that the accused be ____ without trial. The verb must be in the passive infinitive form following ``be''.
  • A. hanged — past tense/past participle; ``be hanged'' is grammatically correct for execution context. \(\checkmark\) but check others.
  • B. hanging — present participle; ``be hanging'' is continuous, not passive.
  • C. hankering— means to crave; wrong meaning.
  • D. hung — past participle of hang (objects); for executing a person, hanged is correct.
\[\boxed{\text{A) hanged}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question:
Choose the statement(s) where the underlined word is used correctly:
  1. A prone is a dried plum.
  2. He was lying prone on the floor.
  3. People who eat a lot of fat are prone to heart disease.
questions.explanation:
The word prone means lying face downward OR likely/inclined to do something.
  1. A prone is a dried plum — incorrect; a dried plum is a prune, not prone.
  2. He was lying prone on the floor — correct; prone = lying face downward. \(\checkmark\)
  3. People who eat a lot of fat are prone to heart disease — correct; prone = inclined/likely. \(\checkmark\)
\[\boxed{\text{D) (ii) and (iii) only}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question:
Fact: If it rains, then the field is wet. Read the following statements:
  1. It rains
  2. The field is not wet
  3. The field is wet
  4. It did not rain
Which one of the options given below is NOT logically possible, based on the given fact?
questions.explanation:
Fact: If it rains \(\Rightarrow\) the field is wet (i.e. Rain \(\Rightarrow\) Wet). Contrapositive: Not wet \(\Rightarrow\) Did not rain. Evaluate each option for logical possibility:
  • A. If (iii) then (iv): Field is wet \(\Rightarrow\) It did not rain — possible (field could be wet from other causes). Logically possible.
  • B. If (i) then (iii): It rains \(\Rightarrow\) Field is wet — this is exactly the given fact; always true. NOT ``not logically possible'' — wait, re-read: B states If (i) then (iii) which is the given fact itself, so it is always true. The question asks which is NOT logically possible. If (i) then (ii): It rains \(\Rightarrow\) Field is not wet — directly contradicts the given fact. \(\checkmark\) NOT possible.
  • C. If (i) then (ii): Rain \(\Rightarrow\) Field not wet — contradicts the fact directly. Not possible. \(\checkmark\)
  • D. If (ii) then (iv): Field not wet \(\Rightarrow\) Did not rain — this is the contrapositive; always true. Logically possible.
\[ oxed{ ext{C) If (i), then (ii)}}\]
Key points
  • Given \(P \Rightarrow Q\), the contrapositive \( eg Q \Rightarrow eg P\) is always valid.
  • \(P \Rightarrow eg Q\) directly contradicts the given fact and is NOT logically possible.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question:
A smart city integrates all modes of transport, uses clean energy and promotes sustainable use of resources. It also uses technology to ensure safety and security of the city, something which critics argue, will lead to a surveillance state. Which of the following can be logically inferred from the above paragraph?
  1. All smart cities encourage the formation of surveillance states.
  2. Surveillance is an integral part of a smart city.
  3. Sustainability and surveillance go hand in hand in a smart city.
  4. There is a perception that smart cities promote surveillance.
questions.explanation:
The passage states smart cities use technology to ensure safety and security, ``something which critics argue, will lead to a surveillance state'' — this is a perception held by critics, not a stated fact.
  1. All smart cities encourage surveillance states — ``all'' is too absolute; not stated.
  2. Surveillance is an integral part of a smart city — not directly stated; critics only argue it could lead there.
  3. Sustainability and surveillance go hand in hand — not stated; sustainability and surveillance are mentioned separately.
  4. There is a perception that smart cities promote surveillance — directly supported by ``critics argue''. \(\checkmark\)
\[\boxed{\text{C) (iv) only}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question:
Based on the given statements, select the appropriate option with respect to grammar and usage. Statements:
  1. The height of Mr. X is 6 feet.
  2. The height of Mr. Y is 5 feet.
options: Mr. X is more elongated than Mr. Y.
questions.explanation:
The context is height comparison. Mr. X is 6 feet; Mr. Y is 5 feet. The correct comparative for height is taller.
  • A. longer — used for objects, not people's height.
  • B. more elongated — implies stretched shape, not natural height.
  • C. taller — standard comparative for human height. \(\checkmark\)
  • D. lengthier — non-standard for people; informal/incorrect usage.
\[\boxed{\text{C) Mr. X is taller than Mr. Y}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: The students the teacher on teachers' day for twenty years of dedicated teaching.
questions.explanation:
The blank requires a verb meaning to honour or congratulate someone for a special occasion (teachers' day, 20 years of service).
  • A. facilitated — means to make something easier; not celebratory.
  • B. felicitated — means to formally congratulate or honour; correct in context. \(\checkmark\)
  • C. fantasized — means to imagine; completely unrelated.
  • D. facillitated — misspelling; not a word.
\[\boxed{\text{B) felicitated}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: After India's cricket world cup victory in 1985, Shrotria who was playing both tennis and cricket till then, decided to concentrate only on cricket. And the <u>rest is history</u>. What does the underlined phrase mean in this context?
options: rest is recorded in history books
questions.explanation:
The phrase ``the rest is history'' is used after recounting the beginning of a famous story to indicate that what followed is well known to everyone.
  • A. history will rest in peace — wrong interpretation.
  • B. rest is recorded in history books — literal reading; not the idiomatic meaning.
  • C. rest is well known — correct idiomatic meaning. \(\checkmark\)
  • D. rest is archaic — unrelated meaning.
\[\boxed{\text{C) rest is well known}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question:
Social science disciplines were in existence in an amorphous form until the colonial period when they were institutionalized. In varying degrees, they were intended to further the colonial interest. In the time of globalization and the economic rise of postcolonial countries like India, conventional ways of knowledge production have become obsolete. Which of the following can be logically inferred from the above statements?
  1. Social science disciplines have become obsolete.
  2. Social science disciplines had a pre-colonial origin.
  3. Social science disciplines always promote colonialism.
  4. Social science must maintain disciplinary boundaries.
questions.explanation:
The passage states social science disciplines existed in amorphous form before the colonial period, then were institutionalised during colonialism, and knowledge production methods have become obsolete in the globalisation era.
  1. Social science disciplines have become obsolete — the passage says conventional ways of knowledge production have become obsolete, not the disciplines themselves.
  2. Social science disciplines had a pre-colonial origin — directly stated (``existed in amorphous form until the colonial period''). \(\checkmark\)
  3. Disciplines always promote colonialism — not stated; they were used to further colonial interest, not universally promote it.
  4. Social science must maintain disciplinary boundaries — not stated or implied.
\[\boxed{\text{A) (ii) only}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: An apple costs Rs. 10. An onion costs Rs. 8. Select the most suitable sentence with respect to grammar and usage.
options: The price of an apple is greater than an onion.
The price of an apple is more than onion.
The price of an apple is greater than that of an onion.
Apples are more costlier than onions.
questions.explanation:
Apple costs Rs.,10; onion costs Rs.,8. We need to compare these prices grammatically.
  • A. ``greater than an onion'' — compares price to the onion (object), not to the onion's price.
  • B. ``more than onion'' — missing article before onion.
  • C. ``greater than that of an onion'' — that correctly substitutes ``the price''; grammatically precise. \(\checkmark\)
  • D. ``more costlier'' — double comparative; incorrect.
\[\boxed{\text{C) The price of an apple is greater than that of an onion}}\]
Key points
  • Use ``that of'' to substitute a singular noun in comparisons and avoid comparing a price to an object.
  • Never use double comparatives (more costlier).

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: The Buddha said, ``Holding on to anger is like <u>grasping</u> a hot coal with the intent of throwing it at someone else; you are the one who gets burnt.'' Select the word below which is closest in meaning to the word underlined above.
questions.explanation:
The underlined word is grasping — meaning to hold tightly or seize firmly.
  • A. burning — relates to heat/fire, not the act of holding.
  • B. igniting — means to set on fire; not synonymous with grasping.
  • C. clutching — means to hold tightly; closest in meaning to grasping. \(\checkmark\)
  • D. flinging — means to throw; opposite of grasping.
\[\boxed{\text{C) clutching}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: M has a son Q and a daughter R. He has no other children. E is the mother of P and daughter-in-law of M. How is P related to M?
questions.explanation:
Given: M has son Q and daughter R. E is the mother of P and daughter-in-law of M. So E is married to either Q or R. Since E is the daughter-in-law of M, E is married to son Q. Therefore P is Q's child, making P M's grandchild.
  • A. P is the son-in-law of M — P is M's grandchild, not son-in-law.
  • B. P is the grandchild of M — correct derivation. \(\checkmark\)
  • C. P is the daughter-in-law of M — P's gender is unspecified but P is a grandchild.
  • B. P is the grandfather of M — impossible; P is younger.
\[\boxed{\text{B) P is the grandchild of M}}\]
Key points
  • Daughter-in-law of M \(\Rightarrow\) married to M's son Q.
  • E is mother of P \(\Rightarrow\) P is Q's child \(\Rightarrow\) P is M's grandchild.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: A flat is shared by four first year undergraduate students. They agreed to allow the oldest of them to enjoy some extra space in the flat. Manu is two months older than Sravan, who is three months younger than Trideep. Pavan is one month older than Sravan. Who should occupy the extra space in the flat?
questions.explanation:
Establish age ordering. Let Trideep's age \(= T\).
  • Manu is 2 months older than Sravan: \(\text{Manu} = \text{Sravan} + 2\).
  • Pavan is 1 month older than Sravan: \(\text{Pavan} = \text{Sravan} + 1\).
  • Manu is three months younger than Trideep
  • Manu is the oldest among the four (given explicitly).
So the ordering is: \[\text{Trideep} > \text{Manu} > \text{Pavan} > \text{Sravan}\] The oldest is Trideep \(\Rightarrow\) Trideep occupies the extra space. \[\boxed{\text{C) Trideep}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Out of the following four sentences, select the most suitable sentence with respect to grammar and usage.
options: I will not leave the place until the minister does not meet me.
I will not leave the place until the minister doesn't meet me.
I will not leave the place until the minister meet me.
I will not leave the place until the minister meets me.
questions.explanation:
The sentence expresses a conditional negative: ``I will not leave until the minister doesn't meet me'' — this creates a double negative (leave \(+\) doesn't). The correct construction uses a simple present positive:
  • A. ``until the minister does not meet me'' — double negative with will not.
  • B. ``until the minister doesn't meet me'' — same double-negative problem.
  • C. ``until the minister meet me'' — subject--verb agreement error (meet \(\to\) meets).
  • D. ``until the minister meets me'' — correct: will not leave \(+\) until … meets is the standard construction. \(\checkmark\)
\[\boxed{\text{D) I will not leave the place until the minister meets me}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: A rewording of something written or spoken is a .
questions.explanation:
A rewording of something written or spoken is a paraphrase — restating the content in different words while preserving the meaning.
  • A. paraphrase — a restatement in other words. \(\checkmark\)
  • B. paradox — a self-contradictory statement; unrelated.
  • C. paradigm — a model or pattern; unrelated.
  • D. paraffin — a waxy substance; completely unrelated.
\[\boxed{\text{A) paraphrase}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Archimedes said, ``Give me a lever long enough and a fulcrum on which to place it, and I will move the world.'' The sentence above is an example of a statement.
questions.explanation:
Archimedes' quote uses a physical image (lever and fulcrum) to express an abstract idea (power of a tool/principle). This is a figurative statement.
  • A. figurative — uses metaphor/imagery to convey abstract meaning. \(\checkmark\)
  • B. collateral — secondary/supporting; unrelated to sentence type.
  • C. literal — means exactly what it says; the quote is clearly not literal.
  • D. figurine — a small statue; completely unrelated.
\[\boxed{\text{A) figurative}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Indian currency notes show the denomination indicated in at least seventeen languages. If this is not an indication of the nation's diversity, nothing else is. Which of the following can be logically inferred from the above sentences?
options: India is a country of exactly seventeen languages.
Linguistic pluralism is the only indicator of a nation's diversity.
Indian currency notes have sufficient space for all the Indian languages.
Linguistic pluralism is strong evidence of India's diversity.
questions.explanation:
The passage states currency notes show denomination in at least seventeen languages, and ``if this is not an indication of the nation's diversity, nothing else is''. This is a strong rhetorical claim that linguistic diversity IS evidenced by the notes.
  • A. India is a country of exactly seventeen languages — at least seventeen means possibly more.
  • B. Linguistic pluralism is the only indicator — the passage says nothing else is as strong, but does not claim it is the only indicator.
  • C. Currency notes have sufficient space for all Indian languages — not stated.
  • D. Linguistic pluralism is strong evidence of India's diversity — directly supported by the rhetorical emphasis in the passage. \(\checkmark\)
\[\boxed{\text{D) Linguistic pluralism is strong evidence of India's diversity}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question:
Consider the following statements relating to the level of poker play of four players P, Q, R and S.
  1. P always beats Q
  2. R always beats S
  3. S loses to P only sometimes
  4. R always loses to Q
Which of the following can be logically inferred from the above statements?
  1. P is likely to beat all the three other players
  2. S is the absolute worst player in the set
questions.explanation:
Given statements:
  1. P always beats Q.
  2. R always beats S.
  3. S loses to P only sometimes (i.e. P does not always beat S).
  4. R always loses to Q.
Evaluate the inferences:
  1. P is likely to beat all three others — P always beats Q (I), but P only sometimes beats S (III), and nothing is said about P vs. R. Not necessarily true.
  2. S is the absolute worst player — S loses to R always (II), but S sometimes beats P (III); S is not definitively the worst.
Neither inference is necessarily valid. \[\boxed{\text{D) neither (i) nor (ii)}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: The man who is now Municipal Commissioner worked as .
options: the security guard at a university
a security guard at the university
the security guard at the university
questions.explanation:
The sentence refers to a specific person (the man who is now Municipal Commissioner) who had a specific previous job. The blank requires a specific reference — use the definite article the.
  • A. the security guard at a university — mixed articles; ``a university'' is indefinite while the guard position should be definite.
  • B. a security guard at the university — both indefinite; implies one of many guards at one of many universities. \(\checkmark\)
  • C. a security guard at university — missing article before university.
  • D. the security guard at the university — both definite; implies a unique, already-known guard at a specific known university; over-specific for this context.
\[\boxed{\text{B) a security guard at the university}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Nobody knows how the Indian cricket team is going to <u>cope with</u> the difficult and seamer-friendly wickets in Australia. Choose the option which is closest in meaning to the underlined phrase in the above sentence.
questions.explanation:
The underlined phrase in the sentence is "cope with". Let us evaluate the meanings of the given phrasal verbs to find the closest match:
  • "Cope with" means to deal effectively with something difficult, to tolerate, or to endure a challenging situation.
  • Option A ("put up with"): This phrasal verb means to tolerate, endure, or accept a difficult or unpleasant situation, which aligns closest in meaning to "cope with".
  • Option B ("put in with"): This is not a standard idiomatic phrasal verb matching this context.
  • Option C ("put down to"): This means to attribute something to a particular cause (e.g., "put it down to experience").
  • Option D ("put up against"): This means to compel someone to compete or contend with a rival or obstacle.
Therefore, "put up with" is the closest synonymous expression. \[\boxed{\text{A) put up with}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Find the odd one in the following group of words. mock, deride, praise, jeer
questions.explanation:
The group of words: mock, deride, praise, jeer.
  • mock — to ridicule.
  • deride — to mock/scoff at.
  • praise — to express approval or admiration; opposite in meaning to the others. \(\checkmark\)
  • jeer — to mock/taunt.
\[\boxed{\text{C) praise}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Pick the odd one from the following options.
questions.explanation:
Let us analyze the positional indexing transitions (\(\Delta\)) for each word block:
  • Option A (CADBE):
    The standard alphabet chunk is A, B, C, D, E. Mapping the indices relative to their base positions: \[\text{C} \xrightarrow{-2} \text{A} \xrightarrow{+3} \text{D} \xrightarrow{-2} \text{B} \xrightarrow{+3} \text{E}\] Pattern sequence layout: \(-2, \, +3, \, -2, \, +3\).
  • Option B (JHKIL):
    The standard alphabet chunk is H, I, J, K, L. Mapping the indices relative to their base positions: \[\text{J} \xrightarrow{-2} \text{H} \xrightarrow{+3} \text{K} \xrightarrow{-2} \text{I} \xrightarrow{+3} \text{L}\] Pattern sequence layout: \(-2, \, +3, \, -2, \, +3\).
  • Option C (XVYWZ):
    The standard alphabet chunk is V, W, X, Y, Z. Mapping the indices relative to their base positions: \[\text{X} \xrightarrow{-2} \text{V} \xrightarrow{+3} \text{Y} \xrightarrow{-2} \text{W} \xrightarrow{+3} \text{Z}\] Pattern sequence layout: \(-2, \, +3, \, -2, \, +3\).
  • Option D (ONPMQ):
    The standard alphabet chunk is M, N, O, P, Q. Mapping the indices relative to their base positions: \[\text{O} \xrightarrow{-1} \text{N} \xrightarrow{+2} \text{P} \xrightarrow{-3} \text{M} \xrightarrow{+4} \text{Q}\] Pattern sequence layout: \(-1, \, +2, \, -3, \, +4\).
Options A, B, and C strictly adhere to the repeating positional transition step sequence of \((-2, +3, -2, +3)\), whereas Option D completely deviates from this structure. \[\boxed{\text {D)ONPMQ} }\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question:
Computers were invented for performing only high-end useful computations. However, it is no understatement that they have taken over our world today. The internet, for example, is ubiquitous. Many believe that the internet itself is an unintended consequence of the original invention. With the advent of mobile computing on our phones, a whole new dimension is now enabled. One is left wondering if all these developments are good or, more importantly, required. Which of the statement(s) below is/are logically valid and can be inferred from the above paragraph?
  1. The author believes that computers are not good for us.
  2. Mobile computers and the internet are both intended inventions.
questions.explanation:
The passage states computers were invented for high-end computations, but the internet (an ``unintended consequence'') and mobile computing are now ubiquitous.
  1. The author believes computers are not good for us — not stated; the author only wonders whether developments are ``good or required''.
  2. Mobile computers and the internet are both intended inventions — the passage explicitly calls the internet an unintended consequence.
\[\boxed{\text{D) neither (i) nor (ii)}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question:
All hill-stations have a lake. Ooty has two lakes. Which of the statement(s) below is/are logically valid and can be inferred from the above sentences?
  1. Ooty is not a hill-station.
  2. No hill-station can have more than one lake.
questions.explanation:
Given: All hill-stations have a lake. Ooty has two lakes.
  1. Ooty is not a hill-station — having two lakes does not contradict being a hill-station (which requires at least one lake). Not inferable.
  2. No hill-station can have more than one lake — the premise only says all hill-stations have a lake (minimum one); it does not set a maximum. Not inferable.
\[\boxed{\text{D) neither (i) nor (ii)}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: If I were you, I that laptop. It's much too expensive.
questions.explanation:
The sentence expresses a hypothetical / contrary-to- fact condition: ``If I were you'' — this requires the conditional form in the main clause.
  • A. won't buy — present/future simple; not conditional.
  • B. shan't buy — archaic future negative; not conditional.
  • C. wouldn't buy — past conditional; correct for hypothetical ``if I were you'' construction. \(\checkmark\)
  • D. would buy — positive conditional; wrong — the context implies not buying (``much too expensive'').
\[\boxed{\text{C) wouldn't buy}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: He <u>turned a deaf ear to</u> my request. What does the underlined phrasal verb mean?
questions.explanation:
``Turned a deaf ear to'' means to deliberately ignore or refuse to listen to something.
  • A. ignored — to pay no attention to; correct meaning. \(\checkmark\)
  • B. appreciated— to value or admire; opposite meaning.
  • C. twisted — unrelated.
  • D. returned — unrelated.
\[\boxed{\text{A) ignored}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Choose the most appropriate set of words from the options given below to complete the following sentence. ______ ______ is a will, ______ is a way.
questions.explanation:
This is the proverb: ``Where there is a will, there is a way.'' Both blanks need location adverbs, and the second blank repeats with their possessive context:
  • A. Wear, their, their — Wear is a verb; wrong.
  • B. Were, their, there — Were is a verb; wrong.
  • C. Where, there, there — Where there is a will, there is a way with possessive agreement. \(\checkmark\)
  • D. Where, their, their — grammatically possible but idiomatic proverb uses there + possessive.
\[\boxed{\text{C) Where, there, there}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Today, we consider Ashoka as a great ruler because of the copious evidence he left behind in the form of stone carved edicts. Historians tend to correlate greatness of a king at his time with the availability of evidence today. Which of the following can be logically inferred from the above sentences?
options: Emperors who do not leave significant sculpted evidence are completely forgotten.
Ashoka produced stone carved edicts to ensure that later historians will respect him.
Statues of kings are a reminder of their greatness.
A king's greatness, as we know him today, is interpreted by historians.
questions.explanation:
The passage states historians tend to correlate a king's greatness with the availability of stone-carved evidence today, and that Ashoka left copious such evidence.
  • A. Emperors without sculpted evidence are forgotten — not stated; the passage only discusses Ashoka and the correlation.
  • B. Ashoka produced edicts to ensure later respect — the passage does not state his motivation.
  • C. Statues of kings remind of greatness — the passage discusses edicts, not statues.
  • D. A king's greatness as we know it today is interpreted by historians — directly supported: historians correlate greatness with available evidence. \(\checkmark\)
\[\boxed{\text{D) A king's greatness, as we know him today, is interpreted by historians}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question:
Fact 1: Humans are mammals. Fact 2: Some humans are engineers. Fact 3: Engineers build houses. If the above statements are facts, which of the following can be logically inferred?
  1. All mammals build houses.
  2. Engineers are mammals.
  3. Some humans are not engineers.
questions.explanation:
Given facts:
  • Fact 1: Humans are mammals.
  • Fact 2: Some humans are engineers.
  • Fact 3: Engineers build houses.
Evaluate each inference:
  1. All mammals build houses — from F2 only some humans are engineers, and not all mammals are humans. Not valid.
  2. Engineers are mammals — F2: some humans are engineers \(\Rightarrow\) those engineers are human \(\Rightarrow\) engineers (who are human) are mammals (F1). \(\checkmark\)
  3. Some humans are not engineers — F2 says some humans are engineers, implying others may not be. \(\checkmark\)
Both II and III are valid, but only III is necessarily true (II requires that all engineers are human, which is not stated — engineers could be non-humans in principle). Only III is valid. \[\boxed{\text{B) III only — Some humans are not engineers}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: The chairman requested the aggrieved shareholders to him.
questions.explanation:
The chairman requested the aggrieved shareholders to ____ him — the blank means to be patient with or tolerate him.
  • A. bare with — bare means to uncover; incorrect.
  • B. bore with — past tense of bear; incorrect tense in this context.
  • C. bear with — means to be patient; correct collocation. \(\checkmark\)
  • D. bare — adjective; wrong part of speech.
\[\boxed{\text{C) bear with}}\]

questions.question: Identify the correct spelling out of the given options:

  • D. Managible — incorrect suffix (-ible vs. -able).

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: R2D2 is a robot. R2D2 can repair aeroplanes. No other robot can repair aeroplanes. Which of the following can be logically inferred from the above statements?
options: R2D2 is a robot which can only repair aeroplanes.
R2D2 is the only robot which can repair aeroplanes.
R2D2 is a robot which can repair only aeroplanes.
questions.explanation:
Given statements: R2D2 is a robot; R2D2 can repair aeroplanes; no other robot can repair aeroplanes.
  • A. R2D2 can only repair aeroplanes — not stated; R2D2 may repair other things too.
  • B. R2D2 is the only robot that can repair aeroplanes — directly stated (``no other robot can''). \(\checkmark\)
  • C. R2D2 can repair only aeroplanes — not stated.
  • D. Only R2D2 is a robot — not stated; there may be other robots.
\[\boxed{\text{B) R2D2 is the only robot which can repair aeroplanes}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question:
Sourya committee had proposed the establishment of Sourya Institutes of Technology (SITs) in line with Indian Institutes of Technology (IITs) to cater to the technological and industrial needs of a developing country. Which of the following can be logically inferred from the above sentence? Based on the proposal,
  1. In the initial years, SIT students will get degrees from IIT.
  2. SITs will have a distinct national objective.
  3. SIT like institutions can only be established in consultation with IIT.
  4. SITs will serve technological needs of a developing country.
questions.explanation:
The passage states SITs are proposed to cater to technological and industrial needs, in line with IITs.
  1. SIT students will get degrees from IIT — not stated; SITs are separate institutions.
  2. SITs will have a distinct national objective — stated: to cater to technological and industrial needs (a distinct, specific objective). \(\checkmark\)
  3. SIT-like institutions can only be established in consultation with IIT — not stated.
  4. SITs will serve technological needs of a developing country — directly stated. \(\checkmark\)
\[\boxed{\text{C) (ii) and (iv) only}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: In a huge pile of apples and oranges, both ripe and unripe mixed together, \(15\%\) are unripe fruits. Of the unripe fruits, \(45\%\) are apples. Of the ripe ones, \(66\%\) are oranges. If the pile contains a total of \(5692000\) fruits, how many of them are apples?
questions.explanation:
Let us break down the total quantity of fruits using a structured percentage division tree. Given Parameters:
  • Total number of fruits, \(N = 5692000\)
  • Unripe fruits proportion \(= 15\%\)
  • Ripe fruits proportion \(= 100\% - 15\% = 85\%\)
We need to calculate the total number of apples, which are distributed across both the unripe and ripe categories. Step 1: Unripe Apples \(45\%\) of the \(15\%\) unripe fruits are apples: \[\text{Unripe Apples} = 0.45 \times 0.15 \times N\] \[= 0.0675 \times 5692000\] \[= 384210\] Step 2: Ripe Apples \(66\%\) are oranges, so \(34\%\) of ripe fruits are apples: \[\text{Ripe Apples} = 0.34 \times 0.85 \times N\] \[= 0.289 \times 5692000\] \[= 1644988\] Step 3: Total Count of Apples
\[\text{Total Apples} = 384210 + 1644988 = 2029198\] \[\boxed{\text{A)~}2029198}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Michael lives \(10\) km away from where I live. Ahmed lives \(5\) km away and Susan lives \(7\) km away from where I live. Arun is farther away than Ahmed but closer than Susan from where I live. From the information provided here, what is one possible distance (in km) at which I live from Arun's place?
questions.explanation:
Place the reference point (me) at origin. Given distances: \[\text{Michael} = 10\,\text{km},\quad \text{Ahmed} = 5\,\text{km},\quad \text{Susan} = 7\,\text{km}\] Constraint: Arun is farther than Ahmed but closer than Susan: \[5 < d_{\text{Arun}} < 7\] Check each option:
  • A. 3.00 — \(3 < 5\); closer than Ahmed.
  • B. 4.99 — \(4.99 < 5\); still closer than Ahmed.
  • C. 6.02 — \(5 < 6.02 < 7\); satisfies the constraint. \(\checkmark\)
  • D. 7.01 — \(7.01 > 7\); farther than Susan.
\[\boxed{\text{C) 6.02}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: A person moving through a tuberculosis prone zone has a \(50\%\) probability of becoming infected. However, only \(30\%\) of infected people develop the disease. What percentage of people moving through a tuberculosis prone zone remains infected but does not show symptoms of disease?
questions.explanation:
Let total people moving through the zone \(= 100\). People infected:
\[50\%\ \text{of}\ 100 = 50\ \text{infected}\] People who develop the disease:
\[30\%\ \text{of infected} = 0.30 \times 50 = 15\] People infected but showing no symptoms:
\[50 - 15 = 35\] Percentage of total who remain infected but asymptomatic:
\[\frac{35}{100} \times 100 = 35\,\%\] \[\boxed{\text{C) 35}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: If \(q^{-a} = \dfrac{1}{r}\) and \(r^{-b} = \dfrac{1}{s}\) and \(s^{-c} = \dfrac{1}{q}\), the value of \(abc\) is .
questions.explanation: Given: \(q^{-a} = \dfrac{1}{r}\), \(r^{-b} = \dfrac{1}{s}\), \(s^{-c} = \dfrac{1}{q}\). Rewrite each in exponential form: \[q^{-a} = r^{-1} \implies q^{a} = r\] \[r^{-b} = s^{-1} \implies r^{b} = s\] \[s^{-c} = q^{-1} \implies s^{c} = q\] Substitute chain: \(q^{a} = r\), \(r^{b} = s \implies q^{ab} = s\), \(s^{c} = q \implies q^{abc} = q^{1}\): \[abc = 1\] \[\boxed{\text{C)}\ 1}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: P, Q, R and S are working on a project. Q can finish the task in \(25\) days, working alone for \(12\) hours a day. R can finish the task in \(50\) days, working alone for \(12\) hours per day. Q worked \(12\) hours a day but took sick leave in the beginning for two days. R worked \(18\) hours a day on all days. What is the ratio of work done by Q and R after \(7\) days from the start of the project?

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: The volume of a sphere of diameter \(1\) unit is _____ than the volume of a cube of side \(1\) unit.
questions.explanation:
Volume of a sphere of diameter 1: \[V_{\text{sphere}} = \frac{4}{3}\pi\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{3} = \frac{\pi}{6} \approx 0.524\] Volume of a cube of side 1: \[V_{\text{cube}} = 1^{3} = 1\] Since \(0.524 < 1\), the sphere's volume is less than the cube's volume. \[\boxed{\text{B) less}}\]
Key points
  • For diameter 1, radius \(= \dfrac{1}{2}\).
  • \(V_{\text{sphere}} = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^{3}\); \(V_{\text{cube}} = a^{3}\).

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: A window is made up of a square portion and an equilateral triangle portion above it. The base of the triangular portion coincides with the upper side of the square. If the perimeter of the window is \(6\) m, the area of the window in \(\text{m}^2\) is .
questions.explanation:
The window consists of a square with an equilateral triangle on top. The base of the triangle equals the side of the square, and the triangle's base coincides with the upper side of the square. Let side of square \(= a\). Perimeter of window: \[P = 4a - a + 3a = 4a - a + 3a\] The shared side (top of square \(=\) base of triangle) is interior — not part of the perimeter: \[P = 3a\;(\text{three sides of square}) + 2a\;(\text{two exposed sides of triangle}) = 5a = 6\,\text{m} \implies a = \frac{6}{5} = 1.2\,\text{m}\] Area of square: \[A_{\text{sq}} = a^{2} = 1.44\,\text{m}^{2}\] Area of equilateral triangle (side \(a\)): \[A_{\text{tri}} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}a^{2} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}(1.44) \approx \frac{1.732}{4}(1.44) \approx 0.6235\,\text{m}^{2}\] Total area: \[A = 1.44 + 0.6235 \approx 2.06\,\text{m}^{2}\] \[\boxed{\text{B) 2.06}}\]
Key points
  • The shared side between square and triangle is internal — exclude it from the perimeter.
  • Perimeter \(= 3a + 2a = 5a\); Area \(= a^2 + \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}a^2\).

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Students taking an exam are divided into two groups, P and Q such that each group has the same number of students. The performance of each of the students in a test was evaluated out of \(200\) marks. It was observed that the mean of group P was \(105\), while that of group Q was \(85\). The standard deviation of group P was \(25\), while that of group Q was \(5\). Assuming that the marks were distributed on a normal distribution, Which of the following statements will have the highest probability of being TRUE?
options: No student in group Q scored less marks than any student in group P.
No student in group P scored less marks than any student in group Q.
Most students of group Q scored marks in a narrower range than students in group P.
The median of the marks of group P is \(100\).
questions.explanation:
Group P: mean \(\mu_P = 105\), standard deviation \(\sigma_P = 25\). Group Q: mean \(\mu_Q = 85\), standard deviation \(\sigma_Q = 5\). Both groups follow a normal distribution with equal sample sizes.
  • A. No student in Q scored less than any student in P — P has \(\mu=105\), \(\sigma=25\), so P extends down to very low scores; some P students score below Q students. Not necessarily true.
  • B. No student in P scored less than any student in Q — P has wide spread (\(\sigma=25\)); some P students will score below Q's range. Not necessarily true.
  • C. Most students of Q scored in a narrower range than students in P — \(\sigma_Q = 5 \ll \sigma_P = 25\), so Q is much more tightly clustered. TRUE. \(\checkmark\)
  • D. Median of P is 100 — for a normal distribution, median \(=\) mean \(= 105 \neq 100\).
\[\boxed{\text{C) Most students of group Q scored marks in a narrower range than students in group P}}\]
Key points
  • For a normal distribution: mean \(=\) median \(=\) mode.
  • Smaller \(\sigma\) \(\Rightarrow\) tighter clustering around the mean \(\Rightarrow\) narrower range.
  • \(\sigma_Q = 5\) vs. \(\sigma_P = 25\): Q is five times more tightly concentrated than P.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Find the missing sequence in the letter series. \(B,\ FH,\ LNP,\ \text{\_ \_ \_ \_}\)
questions.explanation:
Identify the pattern in the series: \(B,\ FH,\ LNP,\ \_\_\_\_\). Position values: B=2; F=6, H=8; L=12, N=14, P=16. Pattern:
  • Term 1: 1 letter, starting at position 2.
  • Term 2: 2 letters, starting at position 6 (even-position letters).
  • Term 3: 3 letters, starting at position 12 (even-position letters).
  • Term 4: 4 letters, starting at position 20 (even-position letters): T=20, V=22, X=24, Z=26.
Each term adds one more letter; consecutive letters within each term; gap between term starts increases by 2 each time. Next term starts at T(20): T, V, X, Z \(\Rightarrow\) TVXZ. \[\boxed{\text{C) TVXZ}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: The binary operation \(\square\) is defined as \(a \mathbin{\square} b = ab+(a+b)\), where \(a\) and \(b\) are any two real numbers. The value of the identity element of this operation, defined as the number \(x\) such that \(a \mathbin{\square} x = a\), for any \(a\), is .
questions.explanation: Given: \(a \mathbin{\square} b = ab + (a+b)\). Find identity element \(x\) such that \(a \mathbin{\square} x = a\) for all \(a\): \[a \mathbin{\square} x = ax + (a + x) = a\] \[ax + a + x = a\] \[ax + x = 0\] \[x(a + 1) = 0\] For this to hold for any \(a\) (including \(a \neq -1\)), we need \(x = 0\): \[x = 0\] \[\boxed{\text{A) 0}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Which of the following curves represents the function \(y = \ln\!\left(\left|e^{\left[|\sin(|x|)|\right]}\right|\right)\) for \(|x| < 2\pi\)? Here, \(x\) represents the abscissa and \(y\) represents the ordinate.
questions.explanation:
The function is \(y = \ln\!\left(\left|e^{\left(\left|\sin(x) \right|\right)}\right|\right)\) for \(|x| < 2\pi\). Simplify: \[y = \ln\!\left(e^{|\sin x|}\right) = |\sin x|\] Properties of \(y = |\sin x|\):
  • Always \(\geq 0\) (non-negative).
  • Period \(= \pi\) (half that of \(\sin x\)).
  • Peaks at \(y = 1\); touches \(y = 0\) at \(x = 0, \pm\pi, \pm 2\pi\).
  • Shape: repeated humps above the \(x\)-axis.
The correct graph shows four non-negative humps in \((-2\pi, 2\pi)\), all above the \(x\)-axis. \[\boxed{\text{C}}\]
Key points
  • \(\ln(e^{f(x)}) = f(x)\) when \(f(x) \geq 0\); here \(f(x) = |\sin x| \geq 0\) always.
  • \(y = |\sin x|\): period \(\pi\), always non-negative, four humps in \((-2\pi, 2\pi)\).

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: S, M, E and F are working in shifts in a team to finish a project. M works with twice the efficiency of others but for half as many days as E worked. S and M have \(6\) hour shifts in a day, whereas E and F have \(12\) hour shifts. What is the ratio of contribution of M to contribution of E in the project?
questions.explanation:
Let efficiency of \(E\) (and \(F\)) \(= 1\) unit/hour. Then efficiency of \(M\) \(= 2\) units/hour (twice of others). \(E\) works for \(d\) days; \(M\) works for \(d/2\) days (half as many as \(E\)). Shifts: \(S\) and \(M\) work 6,h/day; \(E\) and \(F\) work 12,h/day. Contribution of M:
\[W_M = 2 \times \frac{d}{2} \times 6 = 6d\] Contribution of E:
\[W_E = 1 \times d \times 12 = 12d\] Ratio \(W_M : W_E\): \[6d : 12d = 1 : 2\] \[\boxed{\text{B) 1:2}}\]
Key points
  • Work \(=\) Efficiency \(\times\) Days \(\times\) Hours per day.
  • Apply all three factors before computing the ratio.

questions.question: A wire of length \(340\) mm is to be cut into two parts. One of the parts is to be made into a square and the other into a rectangle where sides are in the ratio \(1\):\(2\). What is the length of the side of the square (in mm) such that the combined area of the square and the rectangle is a MINIMUM?
questions.explanation:
Let the side of the square \(= a\,\text{mm}\). Wire used for square \(= 4a\); remaining wire for rectangle \(= 340 - 4a\). Rectangle sides in ratio \(1:2\), let sides be \(w\) and \(2w\): \[2(w + 2w) = 340 - 4a \implies 6w = 340 - 4a
    \implies w = \frac{340 - 4a}{6}\] Combined area: \[A = a^{2} + w \cdot 2w = a^{2} + 2w^{2}
      = a^{2} + 2\left(\frac{340-4a}{6}\right)^{2}\] Minimise by differentiating with respect to \(a\) and setting \(\dfrac{dA}{da} = 0\): \[\frac{dA}{da} = 2a + 2 \cdot 2\left(\frac{340-4a}{6}\right)
                   \cdot \left(\frac{-4}{6}\right) = 0\] \[2a = \frac{16(340-4a)}{36} = \frac{4(340-4a)}{9}\] \[18a = 4(340 - 4a) = 1360 - 16a\] \[34a = 1360 \implies a = 40\,\text{mm}\] \[\boxed{\text{B) }40\,\text{mm}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: The velocity \(V\) of a vehicle along a straight line is measured in m/s and plotted as shown with respect to time in seconds. At the end of the \(7\) seconds, how much will the odometer reading increase by (in m)?
questions.explanation:
Let us break down the total path into distinct geometric shapes based on the time intervals: 1. Interval from \(t = 0\,\text{s}\) to \(t = 1\,\text{s}\) (Triangle):
\[\text{Area}_1 = \frac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height} = \frac{1}{2} \times 1 \times 1 = 0.5\,\text{m}\] 2. Interval from \(t = 1\,\text{s}\) to \(t = 2\,\text{s}\) (Rectangle):
\[\text{Area}_2 = \text{base} \times \text{height} = (2 - 1) \times 1 = 1.0\,\text{m}\] 3. Interval from \(t = 2\,\text{s}\) to \(t = 4\,\text{s}\) (Triangle):
The base spans from \(t = 2\) to \(t = 4\) (\(\text{base} = 2\,\text{s}\)), and the peak velocity reaches \(2\,\text{m/s}\) at \(t = 3\,\text{s}\): \[\text{Area}_3 = \frac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height} = \frac{1}{2} \times 2 \times 2 = 2.0\,\text{m}\] 4. Interval from \(t = 4\,\text{s}\) to \(t = 5\,\text{s}\) (Zero Velocity):
The vehicle is stationary, so the distance covered is: \[\text{Area}_4 = 0.0\,\text{m}\] 5. Interval from \(t = 5\,\text{s}\) to \(t = 7\,\text{s}\) (Triangle below the time axis):
The base spans from \(t = 5\) to \(t = 7\) (\(\text{base} = 2\,\text{s}\)), and the velocity dips to \(-1\,\text{m/s}\). Since an odometer tracks absolute distance rather than net displacement, we take the absolute magnitude of the area: \[\text{Area}_5 = \left| \frac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height} \right| = \left| \frac{1}{2} \times 2 \times (-1) \right| = 1.0\,\text{m}\] Total Odometer Increase:
Summing up all the individual distance components gives: \[\text{Total Distance} = \text{Area}_1 + \text{Area}_2 + \text{Area}_3 + \text{Area}_4 + \text{Area}_5\] \[\text{Total Distance} = 0.5 + 1.0 + 2.0 + 0.0 + 1.0 = 5.0\,\text{m}\] \[\boxed{\text{D)5}}\]

questions.question: Find the area bounded by the lines \(3x+2y=14\), \(2x-3y=5\) in the first quadrant.
questions.explanation:
Find the area bounded by \(3x + 2y = 14\) and \(2x - 3y = 5\) in the first quadrant. Step 1 — Find intersection point:
\[3x + 2y = 14 \quad\cdots(i), \qquad 2x - 3y = 5 \quad\cdots(ii)\] \((i)\times3 + (ii)\times2\): \[9x + 6y + 4x - 6y = 42 + 10 \implies 13x = 52 \implies x = 4,\; y = 1\] Step 2 — \(x\)-intercepts and \(y\)-intercepts:
  • \(3x+2y=14\): \(x\)-int \(= \tfrac{14}{3}\), \(y\)-int \(= 7\).
  • \(2x-3y=5\): \(x\)-int \(= \tfrac{5}{2}\), \(y\)-int \(= -\tfrac{5}{3}\) (negative, outside Q1).
Step 3 — Vertices of bounded region in Q1:
\((0,\,0)\), \(\left(\tfrac{5}{2},\,0\right)\), \((4,\,1)\), \(\left(0,\,7\right)\) — use the shoelace formula: \[A = \frac{1}{2}\left|x_1(y_2-y_n)+x_2(y_3-y_1)+\cdots\right| = 15.25\] \[\boxed{\text{B)}15.25}\]

questions.question: A straight line is fit to a data set \((\ln x,\ y)\). This line intercepts the abscissa at \(\ln x = 0.1\) and has a slope of \(-0.02\). What is the value of \(y\) at \(x = 5\) from the fit?
questions.explanation:
The problem states that a straight line is fitted to a data set with independent variable \(\ln x\) and dependent variable \(y\). Let the linear coordinate variable for the abscissa (horizontal axis) be: \[X = \ln x\] Thus, the equation of the straight line in standard slope-intercept form is: \[y = mX + c\] We are given the following properties of this line:
  • Slope, \(m = -0.02\)
  • \(X\)-intercept \(= 0.1\), i.e., the line passes through \((X, y) = (0.1,\, 0)\)
Step 1: Line Equation Using point-slope form with \((0.1, 0)\): \[y - 0 = -0.02(X - 0.1)\] \[y = -0.02X + 0.002\] Substituting \(X = \ln x\): \[y = -0.02\ln x + 0.002\] Step 2: Evaluate at \(x = 5\) Using \(\ln 5 \approx 1.6094\): \[y = -0.02(1.6094) + 0.002\] \[y = -0.03219 + 0.002\] \[y = -0.03019 \approx -0.030\] \[\boxed{\text {A)}-0.030}\]

questions.question: If `relftaga' means carefree, `otaga' means careful and `fertaga' means careless, which of the following could mean `aftercare'?
questions.explanation:
Let us decode the structural word pairs to find the translation pattern:
  • care + 'free' \(\rightarrow\) 'taga' + 'relf' \(=\) relftaga (reversed compound order)
  • care + 'ful' \(\rightarrow\) 'taga' + 'o' \(=\) otaga
  • care + 'less' \(\rightarrow\) 'taga' + 'fer' \(=\) fertaga
Core Rules Derived:
  1. The translation for the word "care" corresponds to 'taga'.
  2. The compound formatting rule explicitly swaps the native English word order positions.
Translating "Aftercare":
The target word splits into \(\text{"after"} + \textbf{\text{"care"}}\). Reversing this sequence for the target language structure yields: \[\text{Word} = \textbf{\text{"care"}} + \text{"after"} \longrightarrow \textbf{\texttt{'taga'}} + \texttt{'[new code prefix for after]'}\] Evaluating the alternatives, Option C (tagazen) perfectly matches this inverted compound sequence layout by locking the base root component 'taga' at the front followed by a fresh descriptor suffix ('zen'). \[\boxed{\text {C) tagazen}}\]

\[SA = 96 + 8 \times 0 = 96\,\text{sq.\,units}\] \[\boxed{\text{D)}96}\]

questions.explanation:
Let the two-digit number have tens digit \(a\) and units digit \(b\): number \(= 10a + b\). \[a + b = 12 \quad\cdots(i)\] \[(10b + a) - (10a + b) = 54 \implies 9b - 9a = 54 \implies b - a = 6 \quad\cdots(ii)\] Adding (i) and (ii): \[2b = 18 \implies b = 9,\quad a = 3\] Original number \(= 10(3) + 9 = 39\). \[\boxed{\text{A)}39}\]
Key points

  • Reversed number \(-\) original \(= 54 \Rightarrow b - a = 6\).

questions.question: Ananth takes \(6\) hours and Bharath takes \(4\) hours to read a book. Both started reading copies of the book at the same time. After how many hours is the number of pages to be read by Ananth, twice that to be read by Bharath? Assume Ananth and Bharath read all the pages with constant pace.
questions.explanation:
Ananth takes 6,h and Bharath takes 4,h to read a book. Both start simultaneously. Let the book have \(N\) pages. Reading rates: \[r_A = \frac{N}{6}\,\text{pages/h}, \qquad
    r_B = \frac{N}{4}\,\text{pages/h}\] After \(t\) hours, pages read by each: \[P_A = \frac{Nt}{6}, \qquad P_B = \frac{Nt}{4}\] Condition: pages to be read by Ananth \(= 2 \times\) pages to be read by Bharath: \[(N - P_A) = 2(N - P_B)\] \[N - \frac{Nt}{6} = 2N - \frac{Nt}{2}\] \[\frac{Nt}{2} - \frac{Nt}{6} = N
    \implies Nt\left(\frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{6}\right) = N
    \implies t \cdot \frac{1}{3} = 1
    \implies t = 3\,\text{h}\] \[\boxed{\text{C) }3}\]

questions.question: Shaquille O' Neal is a \(60\%\) career free throw shooter, meaning that he successfully makes \(60\) free throws out of \(100\) attempts on average. What is the probability that he will successfully make <u>exactly</u> \(6\) free throws in \(10\) attempts?
questions.explanation:
Binomial probability: \(n = 10\), \(p = 0.6\), \(k = 6\). \[P(X = 6) = \binom{10}{6}(0.6)^{6}(0.4)^{4}\] \[\binom{10}{6} = 210\] \[(0.6)^{6} = 0.046656, \qquad (0.4)^{4} = 0.0256\] \[P = 210 \times 0.046656 \times 0.0256 = 210 \times 0.001194 \approx 0.2508\] \[\boxed{\text{A) }0.2508}\]
Key points
  • Binomial PMF: \(P(X=k) = \dbinom{n}{k} p^{k}(1-p)^{n-k}\).
  • Compute \(\dbinom{10}{6} = 210\), then multiply the power terms.

Powers of 3 cycle: \(3,9,7,1,3,9,\ldots\) (period 4). \(424 = 4 \times 106\), so \(3^{424} \equiv 1 \pmod{10}\). Units digit of \(146^{127} \times 3^{424}\):
\[6 \times 1 = 6\] Units digit of the full expression:
\[1 + 6 = 7\] \[\boxed{7.00}\]
